# App Unified Identity Onboarding (App SSO) Integration Guide

> **English edition** — machine-assisted translation, unified by the i18n PM. **The Chinese original governs.**
> Source: `docs/app-sso-integration.md` · Source baseline: 2026-10-15 · Glossary: [GLOSSARY.md](../GLOSSARY.md) · Governance: [README.md](../README.md)

> Audience: developers embedding the platform's unified identity into in-house enterprise AI applications (Web / H5 / mini-program / desktop / API services).
> This document ships with the service and can be read directly at `http://<platform address>/docs/app-sso-integration.md` (the `/docs` index page lists all published documents).
> Target path: **register the app → get credentials → integrate with the SDK one-liner per the spec → manage business permissions yourself**.

The platform acts as the enterprise's unified identity source (OIDC Provider). Once an app is onboarded:

- The user clicks "Log in" in the app → redirect to the platform authorization page → platform session or login panel (username/password or DingTalk passwordless login, shown/hidden according to the platform's connector configuration) → confirm consent → redirect back to the app with a `code`;
- DingTalk users do not need to log into the platform Console first: on the authorization page's login panel they can scan a DingTalk QR code for passwordless login (first-time identities go through the bind/register branch), then proceed straight to consent;
- The app backend exchanges `code` + `client_secret` for `id_token` / `access_token` (pure-frontend apps use PKCE instead);
- The app calls `userinfo` with the `access_token` to obtain the user identity (`sub` / organization / roles / tenant); **business permissions are the app's own responsibility**;
- If the account is frozen or offboarded on the platform → the app side fails on the very next `userinfo` / `refresh` call; no need to wait for token expiry.

## Interface language note

As of the 2026-10-16 release, the runtime interface (Console, Panel, authorization pages, error messages) ships with a built-in language switcher: Simplified Chinese (default), English (US), and Japanese. Switch via the top-bar selector; the preference is stored in the browser (`rq_lang`). The CLI follows `--lang` or `DSHCTL_LANG`. Any string not yet covered by a dictionary gracefully falls back to Chinese. The bilingual annotations (English name（中文原文）) used in this document remain useful for navigating screenshots and deployments pinned to Chinese.

## 1. Onboarding in five steps

| Step | Action | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Register the app | AI Applications（AI 应用）→ Register App (form factor, access URL, orchestration Agent) | Console（控制台） |
| 2. Issue credentials | App details → SSO Configuration（SSO 配置）tab → Issue SSO Client (`client_id` + `client_secret`; the secret is displayed exactly once) | Console |
| 3. Go-live gate | `web` / `h5` apps cannot go live without an issued SSO client (tunable via `APP_SSO_ENFORCE`); the client's status is re-checked at approval execution time | Console + Approval Center（审批中心） |
| 4. App-side integration | Follow "SDK one-line integration" below, or connect to the endpoints directly — authorization code flow with mandatory PKCE S256 | App code |
| 5. Manage business permissions yourself | `userinfo`'s `sub` is the stable join key; map business roles inside the app | App code |

> **Loopback self-service (no Console needed)**: when the callback address is a local loopback (`127.0.0.1` / `localhost` / `0.0.0.0`), no owner/administrator has to visit the Console on the app's behalf — the app can self-issue the SSO client and retrieve `client_id` / `client_secret` using the machine credential automatically issued at registration (the response is shown only once):
>
> ```
> POST /api/apps/<app ID>/sso-client     (Bearer machine-credential token; the credential includes app.write by default)
> body {"redirectUris":["http://127.0.0.1:5000/oauth/cb"]}
> → 200 { clientId, clientSecret, redirectUris }
> ```
>
> Change callbacks with `PATCH` on the same path; rotate the secret with `POST …/rotate`; the issued configuration (discovery / client_id / callback list, without the secret) is in the `sso` block of `GET /api/apps/:id`. Machine self-service is limited to loopback callbacks; non-loopback callbacks (intranet IPs / public domains) still require the owner or an administrator in the Console (`APP_SSO_MACHINE_LOOPBACK=0` disables this self-service channel entirely).

## 2. SDK one-line integration (recommended)

### Backend / BFF (confidential client, the default form)

Node.js ([openid-client](https://github.com/panva/openid-client) v6 — the same library the platform self-tests with):

```js
import * as oc from 'openid-client'

// 1. One-line discovery-driven setup: just point issuer at the platform address
const config = await oc.discovery(
  new URL('https://sso.yourcompany.com'),        // OIDC_ISSUER (see below)
  process.env.SSO_CLIENT_ID,                     // client_id issued in the Console
  undefined,
  new oc.ClientSecretBasic(process.env.SSO_CLIENT_SECRET),
)

// 2. Login entry: build the authorization URL and 302 (state/PKCE are enforced by the platform)
const verifier = oc.randomPKCECodeVerifier()
const challenge = await oc.calculatePKCECodeChallenge(verifier)
const redirectTo = oc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
  redirect_uri: 'https://your-app.com/auth/cb',  // must match the registered redirect_uris exactly
  scope: 'openid profile email',
  state: oc.randomState(), nonce: oc.randomNonce(),
  code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: 'S256',
})

// 3. At the callback: exchange code for tokens (id_token signature already verified by the SDK via JWKS)
const tokens = await oc.authorizationCodeGrant(config, callbackUrl, {
  code_verifier: verifier, state, nonce,
})
const user = await oc.fetchUserInfo(config, tokens.access_token, tokens.claims().sub)
// user = { sub, name, preferred_username, email?, org: {id,name,tenantId}, roles, tenant }
```

- Silent renewal: `oc.refreshTokenGrant(config, tokens.refresh_token)` (rotation — one use each; replaying an old value revokes the whole chain).
- Logout linkage: `oc.buildEndSessionUrl(config, { id_token_hint, post_logout_redirect_uri, state })`; the platform also revokes that user's refresh chain under this app. When `post_logout_redirect_uri` is omitted and the client has registered exactly one logout redirect, the platform redirects there (passing it explicitly is still recommended; with multiple registered environments this fallback does not apply).
- Active revocation: `oc.tokenRevocation(config, tokens.access_token)` (RFC 7009).

### Pure-frontend SPA (public client — decision D-a: the public form factor is supported)

For H5 / SPA with no backend that cannot hold a secret: choose the **public** client type when issuing — no `client_secret`, **PKCE enforced**, **no refresh token issued** (when the access token expires, silently restart the authorization flow). A suitable frontend library is [oidc-client-ts](https://github.com/authts/oidc-client-ts):

```js
const mgr = new UserManager({
  authority: 'https://sso.yourcompany.com',       // platform discovery address
  client_id: 'oc-xxxxxxxx',                        // public client
  redirect_uri: 'http://localhost:5173/cb',        // localhost debug addresses pass the allowlist
  response_type: 'code', scope: 'openid profile',
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',                   // enforced by the platform
})
await mgr.signinRedirect()                          // login entry
const user = await mgr.signinRedirectCallback()     // at the callback; id_token already verified
```

> Security note: public clients expose a larger token surface; use them only for intranet tools / apps without sensitive data. Prefer confidential (BFF) wherever a backend is possible.

#### CORS (pure-frontend cross-origin calls — allowed by the platform out of the box)

When in-browser JS calls `POST /oauth/token`, `GET /oauth/userinfo`, `POST /oauth/revoke`, and the two discovery endpoints cross-origin, the platform automatically returns CORS allow headers — **no UI configuration needed**:

- Allowed origins = the origin (scheme://host:port) of each registered client `redirect_uri` ∪ the `OIDC_CORS_ORIGINS` environment variable (comma-separated, to append unregistered origins). Registering the callback `http://192.168.0.4:8092/cb` automatically allows `http://192.168.0.4:8092`.
- `OPTIONS` preflight is uniformly 204, with `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization, content-type`; both success and error responses carry `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (browsers can read error bodies).
- Unregistered origins get no allow headers (only `Vary: Origin`); the authorization first hop `/oauth/authorize` and logout `/oauth/end_session` are top-level browser redirects and do not involve CORS.

## 3. Endpoints and discovery

| Endpoint | Path |
|---|---|
| discovery | `GET /.well-known/openid-configuration` |
| JWKS public keys | `GET /.well-known/jwks.json` |
| Authorization | `GET /oauth/authorize` (302 to the platform authorization page) |
| Token exchange | `POST /oauth/token` (`client_secret_basic` / `client_secret_post`; both form-encoded and JSON accepted) |
| User info | `GET /oauth/userinfo` (Bearer access token) |
| Refresh | `POST /oauth/token` (`grant_type=refresh_token`; rotation, scope can only narrow) |
| Revocation | `POST /oauth/revoke` (RFC 7009; always 200) |
| Logout | `GET /oauth/end_session` (`id_token_hint` + `post_logout_redirect_uri`) |

**`OIDC_ISSUER` and intranet / HTTPS reverse proxies**: the default issuer is `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` — local debugging only. In production/intranet deployments you must declare the external address explicitly (behind a reverse proxy, this is the external domain matching the `x-forwarded-host` semantics):

```bash
OIDC_ISSUER=https://sso.yourcompany.com   # discovery/JWKS/endpoints are all built from this
```

Both the app and end-user browsers must be able to reach this address; the reverse proxy must pass through `/oauth/*`, `/.well-known/*`, and the SPA route `/#/oauth/*`. Note: changing the issuer invalidates `iss` checks on existing tokens — expected behavior (token lifetimes are short).

## 4. Claims contract

| claim / field | Semantics |
|---|---|
| `sub` | Platform user ID — **stable, never changes, the single join key** (use it for in-app account mapping; never use username) |
| `preferred_username` / `name` | Username / display name (can be renamed; never use as a primary key) |
| `email` | Returned only when the authorized scope includes `email` |
| `org` / `tenant` | The user's organization `{id,name,tenantId}` / tenant ID (multi-tenant separation reference) |
| `roles` | The user's platform-level role codes on the platform (`super_admin` etc.) — **platform governance roles, not the app's business roles** |
| `id_token.token_use='id'` / `access.token_use='access'` | Token-type tagging: `id_token` proves identity only and cannot call `userinfo` |

"Business permissions are the app's own responsibility": the platform answers "who are you" (identity) plus platform-level permissions over platform resources; in-app menu / data / feature permissions are modeled by the app on top of `sub` (maintain a `sub → business role` mapping table inside the app).

## 5. Security checklist

- **state**: mandatory and echoed back verbatim by the platform (CSRF protection); SDKs handle it automatically — generate and verify it yourself when connecting directly.
- **PKCE S256**: enforced for all clients; `code_challenge` is 43–128 chars base64url.
- **client_secret custody**: store it only in the app backend (environment variables / KMS); rotation lives in the app's SSO Configuration（SSO 配置）; the old value dies immediately.
- **HTTPS**: `redirect_uri` allows `https://` on any host; `http://` is allowed only for intranet addresses (`localhost` / `127.0.0.1` / `0.0.0.0` / `10.x.x.x` / `172.16-31.x.x` / `192.168.x.x`, including intranet IPv6 ULA). Purely intranet deployments may set `APP_SSO_ALLOW_HTTP=1` to allow all http hosts.
- **Machine loopback self-service**: a machine credential bound to the app can self-issue/manage SSO clients whose callbacks are all loopback — local callbacks never cross machines, so under enforced PKCE an intercepted code is worthless to a third party (RFC 8252 posture). Any non-loopback callback requires a human owner / administrator; `APP_SSO_MACHINE_LOOPBACK=0` disables the channel entirely (all operations audited under `app.sso.*`).
- **Logout linkage**: on app logout, call `end_session` so the platform revokes the user's refresh chain under this app (otherwise the app could silently renew after logout). Redirect rule: an explicit `post_logout_redirect_uri` must hit the client's registered logout allowlist (otherwise refused); when omitted and exactly one logout address is registered, that address is used; with none or multiple registered, the user stays on the platform logout page.
- **Freeze = instant invalidation**: freezing / offboarding a platform account → `userinfo` and `refresh` refuse immediately (user status checked in real time).
- **Gate**: `web`/`h5` apps must hold an active SSO client before going live; if the client is disabled while an approval ticket is pending, the execution-time re-check fails.

## 6. Token TTLs (dual-TTL compromise)

| Token | TTL | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Platform Console session access | 30 min | The platform's own security baseline (refresh 7d, rotating) |
| OIDC access token | default 2h (`OIDC_ACCESS_TTL_SECONDS`) | Compromise: app backends verify locally via JWKS; too long enlarges the leak surface, too short fragments the userinfo window |
| OIDC refresh token | default 7d (`OIDC_REFRESH_TTL_SECONDS`) | One-time rotation + whole-chain revocation on replay; frozen/disabled/logged-out → immediately invalid |

## 7. Secret / signing-key rotation runbook

- **App secret rotation**: App details → SSO Configuration（SSO 配置）→ Rotate Secret（轮换 secret）→ the new value is shown once → update the app-side config (the old value 401s immediately). Recommended quarterly, or on suspected leakage.
- **Platform JWKS signing-key rotation**: Authentication & Tokens（认证与令牌）→ Rotate OIDC Signing Key（轮换 OIDC 签名密钥）(requires `authn.oidc.write`). The new key signs immediately; the old key stays valid for verification and published in JWKS for a 24h grace window (in-flight tokens do not drop). SDKs pick the key automatically by `kid` — no app changes needed.
- **Incident response**: suspected token leak → disable the client (authorization/exchange/refresh fail immediately, refresh chain revoked) → rotate the secret → re-enable.

## 8. FAQ

- **Local debugging**: use `http://localhost:<port>/cb`, `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/cb` (or `http://0.0.0.0:<port>/cb`) as `redirect_uri` to pass the allowlist; keep the issuer at the default `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`. Local integration needs no Console access: the app's machine credential self-issues via `POST /api/apps/:id/sso-client` (see §1 "Loopback self-service").
- **Multi-environment issuers**: when one app connects to several platform environments, inject different issuer/client per environment; the `iss` return parameter and the id_token `iss` can be used for mix-up defense.
- **id_token vs userinfo**: if you only need the login identity → verify `id_token` (local JWKS verification) and stop; if you need current organization/roles/status → call `userinfo` (real-time, and freeze-aware).
- **Are the returned `roles` business roles?** No. `roles` are platform governance roles; map business roles inside the app.

## 9. Platform direct entry (entry-ticket — complements app OIDC onboarding)

The Console actions Open Application / Open with Platform Identity（打开应用 / 带平台身份打开应用）no longer redirect naked to `attrs.url`: the logged-in user first collects a one-time entry ticket from the platform, then opens the app at `<url>#entry_ticket=<ticket>`; the app frontend reads the fragment and redeems it with the platform for the platform identity:

```
POST /api/authn/entry-tickets/redeem          (public endpoint; no Bearer required)
body {"ticket":"etk_…"}
→ 200 { refType:"app", refId:"<app ID>", identity:{ sub, username, name, org, roles, tenant } }
```

- Lets apps / UIs that have **not** done OIDC onboarding obtain platform identity with zero changes; apps already onboarded per this guide are unaffected — both channels coexist.
- Tickets are one-time (replay refused), expire after 120s by default (`ENTRY_TICKET_TTL_SECONDS`, adjustable 30–600), and account status is re-checked at redemption; both issuance and redemption are audited (`app.entry.ticket.*`).
- Division of labor vs the standard authorization-code flow: for **long-lived tokens / refresh / standard RP semantics** use `/oauth/authorize` (authorization code + PKCE S256); for **one-shot user identity at entry** use the entry-ticket (no secret, no token exchange; the app backend can integrate later).
- **Error redirects**: authorization failures always 302 to the platform error page (`/#/oauth/error`) and never redirect to an external address (open-redirect protection); declined consent (`consent=false`) redirects back with `error=access_denied` per standard.

## 10. Organization sync endpoint (org-sync; server-to-server)

> Apps that need organization structure only (org tree / department members / department leads) and do not need email can use the default machine-credential self-service channel `GET /api/apps/<appId>/org-sync` — no administrator scope grant needed, and it supports `?ifNoneMatch=` zero-payload change polling. See `docs/app-org-sync.md`. The roster below is for scenarios that need fuller fields such as email.

When an app runs "all-hands filing" style business, it needs an active-employee roster to assign tasks (who receives a filing task, who is the department summarizer). The platform provides a permission-protected roster endpoint that the app backend pulls with a **machine credential** (complementary to the user-login OIDC channel in §1–9: login answers "who is this one person", the roster answers "who does everyone belong to"):

```
GET /api/iam/roster          (Bearer machine-credential token; must include the iam.roster.read permission point)
→ 200 {
  generatedAt: "…",
  orgs:  [{ id, name, parentId, status, leaderUserIds: ["<platform user ID>"] }],   // leaderUserIds come from the DingTalk dept_manager_userid_list sync chain
  users: [{ id, username, displayName, email, jobNumber, title,
            orgId, orgName, primaryOrgId?, status, accountType? }]
}
```

**Three onboarding steps**:

1. **Get the machine credential**: issued automatically at app registration (`refType:'app'`); an administrator adds the scope `iam.roster.read` to the credential in Unified Authentication Center（统一认证中心）→ Identity Principals（身份主体）(changing scopes revokes existing tokens in cascade; it takes effect after the next token exchange).
2. **Token exchange**: `POST /api/auth/client-credentials`, body `{clientId, clientSecret}` → `token` (Bearer).
3. **Pull**: `GET /api/iam/roster`. Pull on the filing cadence (org changes are synced into the platform automatically by the connector on a schedule — see the README's "connector scheduled sync"); do not poll at high frequency.

**Contract highlights**:

- `users[].id` is the `sub` of userinfo — **the same stable join key**; roster-assigned tasks line up directly with identities flowing back from login;
- `orgs[].leaderUserIds` gives each department's leads (synced from the DingTalk "department manager" field), so the app can identify summarizers/approvers without building its own lists;
- PII minimization: no phone numbers; deactivated accounts never appear in the roster; `status` is returned as-is — apps should only assign tasks to `active` accounts;
- Every pull writes an invoke audit record (who pulled how much, when); unauthorized access gets 403 and raises `audit.authz.denied`.

> Memory hook for the division of labor: **login (§1–9) handles "one person arrives"; the roster (this section) handles "everyone exists"**. Both channels join on the user `id`/`sub`; one `sub → business role` mapping table in the app stitches the two together.

## 11. Visitor metrics auto-conversion (platform side) and beacon instrumentation (app side)

The platform automatically folds "SSO-identified visits" and "page views" into app metrics — integrators get DAU with zero effort; one line of beacon instrumentation adds PV/UV.

### Platform-side auto-conversion (zero changes)

| Visit behavior | Conversion | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| entry-ticket redemption (§9) | DAU +1 | Deduplicated per platform `sub` per day |
| OIDC code issuance (consent confirmed on the authorization page, §1–2) | DAU +1 | Deduplicated per platform `sub` per day |
| Browser beacon (below) | PV +1 / UV +1 | PV accumulates per hit; UV deduplicated per `vid` per day |

Multiple same-day visit signals only add, never subtract; they merge naturally via `recordUsage`'s max/accumulate semantics with proactive reporting (`POST /api/apps/:id/metrics-report`) — neither overwrites the other.

### App-side beacon (one line; no machine auth, no secret)

Report once per page load / SPA route change (`<appId>` is the app ID, i.e. the `app_`-prefixed resource ID):

```html
<!-- Option 1: <img> pixel (simplest; cross-origin by nature) -->
<img src="http://<platform address>/api/apps/beacon?app=<appId>&vid=<visitor ID>" hidden alt="">
```

```js
// Option 2: fetch / sendBeacon (POST JSON; when vid is omitted the platform falls back to an IP+UA hash)
const vid = localStorage['rq:vid'] ??= crypto.randomUUID().replace(/-/g, '') // 8-64 char base64url
navigator.sendBeacon?.('/api/apps/beacon',
  new Blob([JSON.stringify({ app: '<appId>', vid })], { type: 'application/json' }))
```

- The endpoint is public (PUBLIC_PATHS) and always returns a 1x1 GIF / `{ok:true}` — unknown apps get the same response, so the endpoint does not reveal app existence;
- `vid`: 8–64 char base64url string; recommended a persistent random ID in `localStorage` (one UV per browser per day);
- Optional `uid`: when the app knows the platform identity (e.g. the `sub` redeemed from an entry-ticket), send it to align UV/DAU accounting;
- Abuse control: per IP per app, counted within 60 requests/minute; over-limit hits are silently ignored (responses still succeed, so pages are unaffected);
- CORS: `*` allowed (GET/POST/OPTIONS) — any entryUrl frontend can report directly.

# Enterprise Deployment & Agent One-Shot Onboarding Runbook

> **English edition** — machine-assisted translation, unified by the i18n PM. **The Chinese original governs.**
> Source: `docs/deploy-enterprise.md` · Source baseline: 2026-10-15 · Glossary: [GLOSSARY.md](../GLOSSARY.md) · Governance: [README.md](../README.md)

> Audience: engineers deploying 元冰可 (YuanBingKe / ybkk-AIOS), the Enterprise AI Resource Management Platform, for an enterprise on top of **DeepSeek Harness (dsh)** — and users who want to hand the deployment/onboarding work **directly to the dsh built-in Agent** to be completed autonomously.
> For day-to-day operations (non-deployment) Agent guidance, see `skills/dsh-ops-admin/SKILL.md` (master index).

## Interface language note

As of the 2026-10-16 release, the runtime interface — Console, Panel, Portal, CLI output, notifications and error messages — ships with a built-in language switcher: Simplified Chinese (default), English (US), and Japanese. Switch via the top-bar selector; the preference is stored in the browser (`rq_lang`). The CLI follows `--lang` or `DSHCTL_LANG`. Any string not yet covered by a dictionary gracefully falls back to Chinese. The bilingual annotations (English name（中文原文）) used throughout this document remain useful for navigating screenshots and on-prem deployments pinned to Chinese, and browser page translation also still works.

---

## 1. Deployment shapes and topology

| Shape | Processes | Description | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Standalone host (default) | `node src/main.ts` | One process provides the REST gateway + Console SPA + a bridge of 41 operations tools (including 4 access-management tools) | Minimal production form; human operation via the Console |
| B. Standalone host + dsh runtime | Shape A process + `dsh web --patch cordis.yml` | The dsh plugin tree exposes all operations tools to models; Agents can operate the platform in natural language. The two processes **share the same `data/` directory**. Form A (standalone host) is the default, SLA-committed form; this form (full dsh runtime) is **experimental** | Enterprises that want Agent-driven operations |
| C. Remote dsh access | Host (A) + `dsh plugin add` on a remote computer | The remote computer installs the platform from the plugin marketplace and applies for a machine credential from the host with a **one-time access code**; all operations tools are proxied remotely to the host for execution (no source code, no shared `data/` needed) | Multiple sites / multiple operators managing the same platform with dsh |

> Key fact: `cordis.yml` does **not** mount the console plugin — the Console SPA and REST are always served by the standalone host process; the dsh side only mounts business plugins (`provideToolRuntime: false`, using dsh's native ToolRuntime).
> Therefore **shape B also requires shape A to be completed first**.

Environment requirements: Node ≥ 22.6 (runs TypeScript natively, no build step); data is persisted in the directory given by `--data` (JSON collections + SQLite `txnstore.db`).

---

## 2. Manual deployment runbook (shape A · executable checklist)

> Every step pairs a command with its expected output: stop if reality does not match, resolve using the troubleshooting note, then continue.

### Step 0: Environment pre-check

- [ ] `node -v` → **v22.6+** (native TS execution, no build step)
      ✘ Below 22.6: upgrade Node first; do not bypass (older versions cannot execute `src/main.ts` directly)

### Step 1: Get the code and dependencies

```bash
git clone <repository URL> ops-platform && cd ops-platform
npm install                # expected: no lines ending in ERR; completes in seconds when package-lock is unchanged
```

### Step 2: First start (baseline initialization wizard)

```bash
# Production: the admin password must be set explicitly (if unset, a random one is generated once and written to data/admin-initial-password.txt)
export ADMIN_PASSWORD='<strong password>'   # Windows PowerShell: $env:ADMIN_PASSWORD='...'
npm start -- --port 7300 --data ./data
```

- [ ] The log shows「平台基线初始化完成」("platform baseline initialization complete") plus the "go-live three steps" guidance box (first start only)
- [ ] The log shows「元冰可|企业AI资源管理平台已启动」("YuanBingKe | Enterprise AI Resource Management Platform started") and the Console address `http://0.0.0.0:7300`
- [ ] `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7300/api/health` → `{"status":"ok",...}`
- [ ] (If `ADMIN_PASSWORD` was not set) confirm `data/admin-initial-password.txt` exists, read it, and **move straight to Step 4 to change the password**

### Step 3: Functional verification

```bash
# Login (expected: response contains a token field)
curl -s -X POST localhost:7300/api/auth/login -H 'content-type: application/json' \
     -d '{"username":"admin","password":"<password>"}'
# First-start state (expected: initialPasswordPending=true — true while the password file is still on the server; false after the password change + file deletion in Step 4)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7300/api/platform/bootstrap
```

- [ ] Login returns a token; opening the Console in a browser shows the yellow "first deployment" banner on the login page (while the password file has not been deleted)
- [ ] Quality gates (isolated instance, production data untouched): `npm run selftest` all green, `npm run lint:manifests` zero errors

### Step 4: Closing takeover (secure the admin account)

- [ ] Change the admin password in the Console: top-right avatar → Change Password（修改密码）
- [ ] Delete `data/admin-initial-password.txt` on the server → `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7300/api/platform/bootstrap` flips to `initialPasswordPending:false` and the login-page banner disappears
- [ ] (Supply-chain hardening, optional but recommended) release-manifest signature verification:

```bash
# Publisher side (one-time): generate a key pair → keep the private key to yourself, register the public key with the platform
node scripts/release-manifest.mjs --generate-key --key-file /secure/release-key.pem
# Administrator side (one-time): register the public key, then enable enforcement (order matters — enabling without a registered public key is rejected)
curl -X POST localhost:7300/api/update/settings -H "authorization: Bearer <token>" \
     -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"releasePublicKey":"<public key base64>"}'
curl -X POST localhost:7300/api/update/settings -H "authorization: Bearer <token>" \
     -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"requireSignedManifests":true}'
```

### Step 5: Process supervision (Linux systemd example)

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/ops-platform.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/opt/ops-platform
Environment=ADMIN_PASSWORD=<strong password>
# Connector gateway gate (if missing, the Connectors page shows "gateway unavailable" and failed probes spam the audit log — test report DEF-02)
Environment=OOMOL_CONNECT_ADMIN_TOKEN=<strong secret>
Environment=OOMOL_CONNECT_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<random string of 32+ bytes>
# Port-occupation guard: an orphan process seizing the port makes restart silently ineffective (test report DEF-04); check before start
ExecStartPre=/opt/ops-platform/scripts/guard-port.sh 7300
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node src/main.ts --port 7300 --data /opt/ops-platform/data
Restart=always
```

Operations essentials:

- **Operations iron rule**: always start/stop the service via `systemctl`; never bypass systemd by hand-launching `node src/main.ts`
  (once an orphan process grabs the port, `systemctl restart` fails or the old process keeps the port — changes never take effect and are hard to diagnose).
- **Backup**: a cold copy of the whole `--data` directory is sufficient (JSON is written atomically + SQLite WAL). Metering data lives in `txnstore.db`.
- **Upgrades (built-in update check since v1.1+)**: by default the platform checks the upstream GitHub repository for a new version every 24h (adjust or disable in the Console top bar Platform Updates（平台更新）drawer, or via `dshctl update set`). When a new version is found, an "updatable" badge appears in the Console top bar and a `platform.update.available` event is broadcast (audit-trailed). Upgrade method depends on the install shape — pick one:
  - **Source checkout (source)**: use the Console drawer's one-click upgrade, or rehearse with `dshctl update apply --dry-run` and then run `dshctl update apply --reason="…"` (internally runs `git pull --ff-only` + `npm install`; it fails safely — without forcing — if local uncommitted changes exist), then `systemctl restart ops-platform` to take effect. Run `npm run selftest` before switching traffic.
  - **Plugin marketplace install (bundle)**: on the host's dsh side run `dsh plugin update github:01men/ybkkasi`, then restart the dsh host.
    (Package source migrated from `github:01men/ybkk-AIOS` to `github:01men/ybkkasi` on 2026-10-14.)
  - An Agent can also simply be told "check platform updates" / "upgrade the platform" in a session (the `update_status` / `update_check` / `update_apply` tools).
- **External publishing**: reverse-proxy port 7300 via Nginx or similar and terminate TLS there; the platform itself authenticates with Bearer tokens.
- **Enterprise customization (as needed)**: DingTalk real connector (`mode: real` + `apiBase`, configured in the Console under Organization & Accounts（组织与账号）→ Third-party Integrations（三方集成）).
  Third-party access supports **multiple entities and multiple instances per provider**: one DingTalk tenant can serve several enterprise entities (each with its own corpId/appKey/appSecret). Configuration is addressed by instance id and unique per `provider|corpId` (duplicate entities are rejected); each instance has independent configure/test/sync/delete, synced departments are owned per connector instance, and login/binding can be initiated per entity. REST surface: `POST /api/iam/connectors` creates an instance, `DELETE /api/iam/connectors/:id` deletes one (permission point `iam.connector.write`); in the existing `PUT/POST /api/iam/connectors/:param[/test|/sync]`, `:param` resolves by instance id first and falls back to the first entry of that provider (enabled entries first) — existing callers are compatible unchanged. New config fields: `name` (entity display name, used in the login entry/list) and `targetOrgId` (root department for the sync tree; empty = platform root). OIDC declares its external address via the `OIDC_ISSUER` environment variable; in production, migrate the OIDC private key to a KMS.
- **Intranet / rate-limited networks**: the update check calls the GitHub API (unauthenticated quota 60 requests/hour/IP; set `GITHUB_TOKEN` to raise it); private mirrors can override the endpoints with the `DSH_UPDATE_API_BASE` / `DSH_UPDATE_RAW_BASE` environment variables.
- **Funding boundary**: payment / corporate transfer / invoicing channels are a manual transitional state; before integrating any, read the "Funding Red Line" section (三A 资金红线) of the repo README. The platform carries **no billing or settlement semantics** (M0 baseline).

---

## 3. dsh runtime onboarding (shape B — enabling Agent operations)

Prerequisite: a usable checkout of deepseek-harness (`pnpm dsh web`).

```bash
# 1. Generate the onboarding overlay (replace <PROJECT_ROOT> with this repository's absolute path)
sed 's|<PROJECT_ROOT>|/opt/ops-platform|g' cordis.yml > /tmp/ops-overlay.yml

# 2. Start inside the deepseek-harness checkout (shares data/ with the standalone host; both processes online)
pnpm dsh web --patch /tmp/ops-overlay.yml
```

Agent operations credentials (environment variables): `DSHCTL_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:7300`), `DSHCTL_USER` / `DSHCTL_PASS` (use an ops-class account; do not keep admin resident), or `DSHCTL_TOKEN`.
For routine operations, just have the Agent read `skills/dsh-ops-admin/SKILL.md` (the loop: diagnose → collect evidence → dry-run rehearsal → execute → verify; L4 high-risk operations automatically go through an approval ticket).

---

## 4. Remote dsh access (shape C: marketplace install → access code → automatic credential application)

Applies when the dsh on another computer has installed this platform via `dsh plugin --profile web add github:01men/ybkkasi` and does not know how to configure credentials/passwords issued by the host. The whole flow requires **no manual editing of any config file on the remote computer**.

### 4.1 Host side: issue a one-time access code (administrator, Console or CLI)

```bash
# Console: log in → left sidebar Platform（平台）→ Platform Access（平台接入）→ Create Access Code (choose template/TTL/remark; the code is displayed exactly once)
# or CLI:
DSHCTL_URL=http://<host IP>:7300 DSHCTL_USER=admin DSHCTL_PASS=*** \
  node cli/dshctl.mjs connect code --template=operator --ttl=15 --remark="R&D, Wang"
```

Permission templates (= the remote client's permission boundary after onboarding):

| Template | Permissions |
|---|---|
| `readonly` (default) | All query-type permission points (list/get/metrics/logs) |
| `operator` | Read-only + MCP/Skill/Agent/application operations and approval decisions; **excludes** account and credential management |
| `full` | All permissions (`*`); trusted environments only |

### 4.2 Remote computer: two onboarding channels (pick either)

```text
(1) Agent channel (recommended): tell the Agent directly in the dsh UI:
    "Onboard to the host platform, address http://<host IP>:7300, access code <enr_…>"
    The Agent will call the connect_setup tool to complete the application automatically and switch the
    37 operations tools to remote execution.

(2) Config page channel: open http://127.0.0.1:7390 in a browser (on the remote computer itself; the plugin
    listens automatically at startup), enter host address + access code → Apply（申请接入）.
    From this page you can later update the configuration, test the connection, or disconnect at any time.
    If a machine credential already exists (mc-/cs_ prefixes), switch to the "existing machine credential" tab.
```

### 4.3 Verification and operations

- Remote side: have the Agent run `connect_status` (should show remote mode, valid token) and `agent_list` (returns host data).
- Host side: the computer appears in the Console under Platform Access（平台接入）→ Connected Clients（已接入客户端）(name/template/hostname/last used).
- Revocation: on the host, "disable client" (reason required, audit-trailed) → all machine tokens are revoked in cascade; remote tool calls immediately get 401. On the remote side, `connect_reset` only clears local credentials.
- Security baseline: access codes are stored hashed (displayed exactly once at creation), consumed on first use, TTL configurable (default 15 minutes), with per-source-IP failure lockout (5 failures per 15-minute window); machine credentials, equivalent to passwords, are stored only on the remote machine (mode 0600); client tool proxying goes through the host's `/api/tools/execute`, with per-tool RBAC checks and full auditing.

### 4.4 FAQ

| Symptom | Resolution |
|---|---|
| `connect_setup` reports "access code invalid" | The code was already used / expired / revoked (one-time consumption); create a new one on the host |
| "Host unreachable" | Check the host listens on 0.0.0.0 and firewall rules; the address must include `http://` and the port |
| Tool execution fails 403 missing permission point | Permission template too narrow; on the host, disable the client and re-onboard with a higher-template access code |
| Remote still shows configured after disabling | Local credential still present but invalid; run `connect_reset` on the remote side to clear it |

---

## 5. One-shot Agent instruction (paste the whole block to the dsh built-in Agent)

> Usage: send the entire instruction block below to the dsh Agent, replacing the `<...>` placeholders; the Agent completes deployment and verification on its own and reports back.
> In production, a human should first confirm the placeholders and password strength; the instructions carry built-in guardrails (no demo data, never overwrite an existing data directory, high-risk operations go through approval).

```text
[TASK] Deploy "YuanBingKe Unified Enterprise AI Resource Management Platform" (元冰可 · 企业 AI 资源统一管理平台)
on <target server, e.g. 10.0.0.5 or this machine> and complete verification.
Repository: <git clone URL, e.g. git@github.com:01men/ybkkasi.git>; deploy directory: <e.g. /opt/ops-platform>;
listen port: <7300>; admin password: <ADMIN_PASSWORD strong password>; attach dsh runtime after deployment: <yes/no>.

[STEPS]
1. Environment check: confirm Node ≥ 22.6 (node -v). If not satisfied, stop and report — do not upgrade
   the system Node on your own.
2. Get the code: clone (or, if the directory exists, git pull) into the deploy directory; record the commit hash.
3. Install dependencies: npm install.
4. Production initialization: set the ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variable; start with --port <port>
   --data <deploy dir>/data (prefer systemd/PM2 supervision). Iron rule: NEVER set DEMO_SEED=1; if the data/
   directory already exists and is non-empty, treat it as an existing instance — stop and ask a human to
   confirm; do not overwrite.
5. Health verification (all must pass to count as success):
   a. GET / returns 200;
   b. POST /api/auth/login (admin + password) returns a token;
   c. GET /api/overview (Bearer token) returns 200;
   d. npm run selftest passes in full; npm run lint:manifests passes with zero errors (pass count as of the latest run).
6. (Optional, only if "attach dsh" = yes) generate the overlay per section 3 of docs/deploy-enterprise.md and
   start with pnpm dsh web --patch; verify both processes share the same data/.
7. Report: commit hash, service address, whether the admin first login succeeded, selftest results, and how the
   initial password was delivered (never paste it in plaintext into public channels).

[GUARDRAILS]
- Every high-risk operation (offline/revoke/delete) must go through a platform approval ticket with an audit
  trail; no bypassing.
- Read-only commands may run freely; rehearse with --dry-run before any change.
- After deployment, change the admin initial password immediately and create enterprise-owned accounts
  (see skills/dsh-ops-iam).
```

## 6. Acceptance checklist

- [ ] `GET /` returns 200 and the Console logs in (admin + `ADMIN_PASSWORD`)
- [ ] `npm run selftest` all green, `npm run lint:manifests` zero errors (counts as of the latest run)
- [ ] The production data directory contains **no** demo data (`data/iam~users.json` has no demo accounts such as ops/hr/dev)
- [ ] `GET /api/platform/bootstrap` returns `initialPasswordPending:false` (initial password takeover completed)
- [ ] (Shape B) `dsh web` is running and the Agent can answer `dshctl mcp list`-style questions
- [ ] (Shape C) the remote computer's `connect_status` shows remote mode; the host's Platform Access（平台接入）page lists the client
- [ ] Backup policy in place (scheduled cold copy of the `data/` directory)
- [ ] The admin initial password has been changed, and the demo password `Ybk@2026` cannot log in
      (demo credentials are for demo environments only — never enable `DEMO_SEED=1` in production)
- [ ] (Optional supply-chain hardening) `GET /api/update/status` shows `releaseKeyConfigured:true`

---

## 7. Regional deployment notes

Added for international readers; framed as capabilities, not certifications.

- **Time zones.** Usage/metering events are stamped in ISO 8601 UTC (`occurred_at`; monthly report windows `[first day of month 00:00, first day of next month 00:00)` in UTC). Platform console logs, by contrast, are written in the server's local time — when operating across regions, convert explicitly and record the server's time zone in your runbook. Report months are passed as `YYYY-MM`.
- **Rate-limited / intranet networks.** The built-in update check calls the GitHub API (unauthenticated: 60 requests/hour/IP). On rate-limited networks set `GITHUB_TOKEN`, or point the platform at a private mirror with `DSH_UPDATE_API_BASE` / `DSH_UPDATE_RAW_BASE`. All other platform traffic stays inside your deployment boundary.
- **Data residency.** The platform is self-hosted by design: with on-premises (private) delivery, all data — identities, metering events, audit logs, SQLite stores — remains inside the enterprise's own boundary; private project-based delivery is available (currently oriented to manufacturing customers). This is a deployment capability statement: no third-party compliance certification (e.g., SOC 2, ISO 27001) is claimed; those are on the roadmap (Roadmap).

# YuanBingKe (ybkk-AIOS) — The DSH Ecosystem


This document explains the ecosystem YuanBingKe lives in: the dsh (DeepSeek Harness) host, the cordis plugin framework, how YuanBingKe mounts into dsh, what a plugin looks like, how the plugin marketplace works, who does what in the ecosystem, and how protocol keys are governed. For the product-level overview see [README.md](README.md); for installation commands see [getting-started.md](getting-started.md).

**Interface language note:** as of the 2026-10-16 release, the runtime interfaces of both YuanBingKe and dsh ship with a built-in language switcher — Simplified Chinese (default), English (US), and Japanese (top-bar selector, `rq_lang` preference; CLI via `--lang` / `DSHCTL_LANG`; strings not yet covered by a dictionary fall back to Chinese). UI locations are annotated bilingually on first mention; protocol keys are ASCII and never translated (Section 7).

## 1. What are dsh and cordis?

**dsh (DeepSeek Harness)** is an agent runtime: it hosts agent sessions behind a web service (`dsh web`), exposes tools to models through its native ToolRuntime, and loads domain skill manuals from `.dsh/skills` directories. Capabilities are added to dsh by installing **plugins** into a profile (for example the `web` profile) — there is no fork-and-patch path.

**cordis** (`@deepseek-ai/cordis`) is the plugin framework underneath dsh. A cordis plugin declares its dependencies and lifecycle; at runtime each plugin receives a context (`ctx`) through which it registers services, routes, and tools. YuanBingKe is built on the **same framework**, which is what makes the "Everything is a plugin" architecture portable between hosts (Section 3).

Two precision points, stated honestly:

- YuanBingKe's cross-plugin event bus (`ctx.platformBus`) is a platform-owned in-memory pub/sub with persistence, retry, dead-letter handling, and source validation — it is not the cordis event system. Third-party code may only emit events namespaced `plugin:<id>:` (Section 7).
- A bundle installation resolves plugins to the **host's own cordis instance**; the repository keeps `@deepseek-ai/cordis` in `devDependencies` only. Two cordis instances in one process cause `ctx.plugin(...)` registrations to silently no-op and the whole service chain (iam → usage → audit ...) to hang in pending — the ecosystem's best-known failure mode.

Ecosystem vocabulary, for readers new to dsh:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Host (宿主) | the process that loads the plugin tree — here, the platform's own process or a dsh `web` process |
| Profile | a dsh-side plugin installation root (`--profile web`); installs resolve along the profile's `node_modules` closure |
| Patch / overlay | a YAML file (`cordis.yml` for source checkouts, `cordis.patch.yml` for bundle installs) that mounts plugin entries into a dsh process at start |
| Mount (挂载) | attaching the YuanBingKe data plane into the dsh webServer under the `/rq` prefix |
| Enrollment code | one-time host-issued credential (`enr_...`) a remote dsh client exchanges for machine credentials |

## 2. "Everything is a plugin"

YuanBingKe's architecture slogan is literal: every business domain is one plugin package. Each plugin independently declares its dependencies, permission points, and events, and can be started and stopped independently. A running platform is a **plugin tree**; a bundle install mounts **25 plugin entries** into a dsh profile in one command.

Plugins collaborate only through events and extension points — a state change must emit an event, and plugins never read each other's storage directly:

| State change | Automatic reaction |
|---|---|
| `iam.user.frozen` | authn revokes all of the user's tokens |
| `agent.offlined` | machine credentials revoked + bound users notified |
| `skill.deprecated` | referencing agents alerted |
| `mcp.unhealthy` | circuit breaking + audit trail |

The full tree with per-plugin descriptions is in [README.md §4](README.md).

## 3. How YuanBingKe mounts into dsh

| Form | What runs where | Entry point | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Independent host | `node src/main.ts` serves REST + Console SPA + tools bridge | platform port (default 7300) | no dsh required; baseline for all other forms |
| Full dsh runtime (source checkout) | same plugin tree patched into `dsh web --patch cordis.yml`, sharing the `data/` directory | both ports | operations tools surface in dsh's native ToolRuntime and become model-callable |
| Bundle mount (recommended for use) | `dsh plugin --profile web add github:01men/ybkkasi` | **dsh web port is the single entry** | the host bridge mounts the YuanBingKe data plane under the `/rq` prefix |

The key piece is **`dsh-plugin-dsh-bridge` (the host bridge)**: it mounts YuanBingKe's data plane — REST, the Console SPA, static docs, and the `/mcp` endpoint — into the dsh webServer under the **`/rq` prefix**, so users and agents reach everything through one port; the platform's own HTTP listener can be turned off with `startHttp: false`. Companion access-layer plugins complete the in-session experience: `dsh-plugin-panel-core` (department Agent workbench Panel（面板）: `/panel` SPA + `/api/panel/*` REST + SSE), `dsh-plugin-rq-card` (four-state execution cards with a thumbs-up / thumbs-down feedback bar injected into dsh conversations — a `dsh.client` dual-sided plugin), and `dsh-plugin-dingtalk-bridge` (DingTalk group bridge, outbound delivery, approval push, alert channels).

Once mounted, the platform's registered **operations tools enter dsh's native ToolRuntime** (the plugins declare `provideToolRuntime: false`, reusing the host runtime instead of the built-in lite one). Models can then operate the whole platform in natural language — "list all MCP services and their health" triggers `mcp_service_list`; "what can be installed from the Skill Marketplace" triggers `skill_search`. The operations tool set counted 37+ tools as of the latest releases; counts evolve release to release, and the different surfaces (dsh ToolRuntime, the REST tools bridge, `/mcp`) expose slightly different supersets — the manifests are the source of truth.

### 3.1 The `tools` seam and service-key de-confliction

Two load-bearing implementation details matter to anyone embedding plugins into dsh:

- The `tools` service key is **deliberately shared**: under the independent host it is provided by ToolRuntime-lite; under dsh it is provided by the native ToolRuntime. All operations tools flow through whichever host supplies it.
- YuanBingKe's JSON storage service key is `opsStorage`, **not** `storage` — the dsh host ships its own `storage` service, and sharing the name caused plugins to receive the wrong service at construction. New ecosystem plugins should follow the same namespacing discipline.

### 3.2 Source-checkout mode (local development)

Developers pointing a dsh source checkout at a YuanBingKe checkout must satisfy two hard requirements:

1. In `cordis.yml`, replace `<PROJECT_ROOT>` with an absolute `file:///` URL (bare Windows drive-letter paths fail ESM resolution with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME`);
2. Link `node_modules/@deepseek-ai/cordis` to the dsh source tree's `vendor/cordis` (a junction on Windows), so plugins and host load **the same cordis instance**.

Then run `pnpm dsh web --patch <project>/cordis.yml` from the dsh checkout. Bundle installs avoid all of this: entries are declared as package name + subpath and resolve along the profile's `node_modules` to the host's cordis closure.

### 3.3 Skills distribution

Domain operations skill manuals (`skills/dsh-ops-*/SKILL.md`, 9 skills, including the `dsh-ops-admin` master index) do not auto-enter dsh's skill system — dsh only scans `.dsh/skills` roots. Host operators distribute them explicitly:

```bash
cp -r skills/dsh-ops-* ~/.dsh/skills/    # user level: available in all sessions
# or project level:
mkdir -p .dsh/skills && cp -r skills/dsh-ops-* .dsh/skills/
```

### 3.4 Remote dsh access (the third form)

For distributed teams, other computers install the bundle from the marketplace and connect back to the host via `dsh-plugin-connect` — no source checkout, no shared data directory:

1. The host admin creates a **one-time enrollment code** on the **Platform Access（平台接入）** page or via CLI (`node cli/dshctl.mjs connect code --template=operator --ttl=15`), choosing a permission template: `readonly` (default), `operator` (adds MCP/skill/agent/app operations and approval decisions; no account or credential management), or `full` (trusted environments only).
2. The remote computer connects either by telling the dsh agent "enroll to host `<URL>` with code `enr_...`" (the agent calls `connect_setup`), or through the local configuration page at `http://127.0.0.1:7390`.
3. After enrollment, the operations tools switch to **host-forwarded execution** (the remote machine holds no data); a heartbeat is pushed to the host every 5 minutes by default (`heartbeatIntervalMinutes=0` disables); the host page lists connected clients with last-use and last-heartbeat, and can disable a client at any time — revoking all its machine tokens immediately.

Security baseline: enrollment codes are stored hashed (shown once at creation), consumed once, TTL-configurable (default 15 minutes), with per-source-IP failure lockout (5 failures per 15 minutes); machine credentials are equivalent to passwords and live only on the remote machine with `0600` permissions.

### 3.5 Choosing a form

- **Just evaluating?** Independent process + `DEMO_SEED=1` (never in production).
- **Want agents to operate the platform in natural language, one entry point?** Bundle mount into your dsh host (`/rq` prefix, dsh web port as the single entry).
- **Developing against a dsh source checkout?** Patch mode (`cordis.yml` + junction), per Section 3.2.
- **Multiple sites or admin workstations?** Bundle install everywhere + remote enrollment against one host (Section 3.4).

## 4. Plugin anatomy

Every first-party plugin follows one layout (translated annotations; identifiers verbatim):

```text
packages/plugin-<name>/
  plugin.yaml             declares: id / version / depends / permissions
  manifest/
    api.yaml              REST routes + tools + service keys — the single source of truth
                          aligned across the REST, tools-bridge, and /mcp surfaces
    permissions.yaml      permission points, registered into the unified RBAC
    events.yaml           published / subscribed events
    ui.yaml               routes + menu entries
    billing.yaml          compatibility-retained metering declaration face: only meter keys
                          and units participate in metering registration; the monetary side
                          is always the zero-price snapshot (M0)
  src/index.ts            services + plugin assembly
  src/tools.ts            model-facing tools (dsh ToolRuntime contract)
```

- **Independent declaration, independent lifecycle.** Because dependencies, permissions, and events are declared, the framework can start/stop plugins independently and the platform can enforce least privilege per plugin.
- **Machine-checked contracts.** `npm run lint:manifests` validates the five manifest faces as YAML and cross-checks declared routes and tools against the code (route / tool contract comparison), catching drift before release.
- **Declarations are generated.** `scripts/gen-manifests.mjs` scaffolds and regenerates manifest faces so code and declaration stay aligned.

The tool layer shows why the contract discipline matters: every tool declared in a plugin's `src/tools.ts` is served with the same contract on three surfaces — the REST tools bridge, the dsh ToolRuntime (form B), and the `/mcp` endpoint — which is why an operator can run the identical call as a CLI command (`node cli/dshctl.mjs tool exec --name=agent_list --args='{"status":"online"}'`), as a model tool call in a dsh session, or as a raw `/mcp` `tools/call` from any MCP client. `manifest/api.yaml` is the source of truth all three are checked against.

Third-party plugins follow the same discipline under a stricter contract (Section 5).

## 5. The plugin marketplace

`dsh-plugin-market` operates a marketplace for **third-party and first-party plugins and skills**.

### 5.1 The five-face contract and Ed25519 verification

A third-party submission ships a five-face contract:

- `plugin.yaml` — metadata: id, version, publisher, signature, dependencies, requested capabilities, sandbox level (L0 only today);
- `manifest/permissions.yaml` — requested permissions, approved item-by-item by the enterprise at install time;
- `manifest/api.yaml` — declarative provision face (registration only at L0; no live routes);
- `manifest/events.yaml` — subscriptions only (third parties may never emit platform-namespace events);
- `manifest/billing.yaml` — metering declaration only; monetary fields have no effect under M0;
- plus a `content/` payload for L0: prompt packs, configuration templates, tool descriptions — **no executable code**.

The publisher signs the content fingerprints with an **Ed25519** private key; the platform verifies against the developer's registered public key before anything is listed.

### 5.2 From developer to installed plugin

1. **Developer identity.** Third-party developers register in a dedicated identity domain inside the marketplace (separated from the internal employee IAM domain, with its own credentials and publisher key pair).
2. **Scaffold, sign, submit.** The CLI does all three:
   ```bash
   node cli/dshctl.mjs plugin init --id=com.demo.hello --dir=./my-plugin   # five-face scaffold + publisher key pair
   node cli/dshctl.mjs plugin sign --dir=./my-plugin
   node cli/dshctl.mjs plugin submit --dir=./my-plugin
   ```
3. **Review gates.** Static content scanning; a marketplace admission gate currently accepts **L0 (declarative) only** — a code-carrying sandbox (L1) is a designed roadmap item, and the gate rejects anything else until that lands; platform admins approve publishing, then installation, per enterprise.
4. **Runtime accountability.** Installed capabilities are frozen into an approved set at install time; a reconciliation job periodically compares actual consumption against declared capabilities, raising `usage.capability.drift` and auto-suspending offenders for review. Any change to L0 content (prompt/config fingerprints) forces a fresh scan and approval.
5. **Versioned publishing.** Every publish is a new immutable version; installation registers dependencies; deprecation warns referencing agents; uninstall is an approved operation too.

### 5.3 Third-party vs first-party

First-party plugins ship inside the platform tree and are metered with **zero-price metering declarations** (the M0-3 posture). Third-party submissions run in a constrained context: events namespaced `plugin:<id>:`, tokens scoped to `plugin:<id>:<cap>` namespaces, platform-service access clipped to approved capabilities by a proxy context. Marketplace prices do not exist — third-party metering declarations register at zero price, and no subscription or revenue-share flows are accepted (M0).

Where you meet the marketplace in practice: developers work in the CLI (`dshctl plugin` and `skill` command groups, Section 5.2); platform admins approve publishes, installs, and uninstalls in the Console（控制台）， where the Skill Marketplace page also carries a skill × day usage heatmap card; agents discover supply in-session through tools such as `skill_search`. Versioned publishing means an installed enterprise always pins an immutable version, and deprecation is announced through events (`skill.deprecated`) rather than silent removals.

## 6. Ecosystem roles

| Role | What they can do |
|---|---|
| **dsh host operators** | Run `dsh web`, install/update plugins into profiles (`dsh plugin --profile web add ...`), mount YuanBingKe via the host bridge, distribute `.dsh/skills` manuals, and operate the platform through agents in session or through `dshctl` |
| **Platform admins** (YuanBingKe side) | Own baseline initialization, RBAC and permission points, L4 approvals, marketplace admission (approving third-party publishes and installs), connector configuration, self-update, and client revocation on the **Platform Access（平台接入）** page |
| **Third-party plugin / skill developers** | Register a developer identity, sign the five-face contract with Ed25519, submit versioned releases through the CLI, and publish declarative (L0) content — always subject to scanning, approval, event namespacing, scoped tokens, and capability reconciliation |

## 7. Protocol governance

The ecosystem is multilingual in documentation but **monolingual in protocol**: cross-system machine contracts stay ASCII in every language edition. Never translate, transliterate, or localize:

1. event names (`platform.update.available`, `flow.*`, `plugin:<id>:*`);
2. permission points (`iam.user.write`, `workforce.admin`, `platform.update.apply`);
3. error reason codes and the `ok` / `data` / `error` API envelope fields;
4. environment variable names (`DEMO_SEED`, `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, `USAGE_RETENTION_DAYS`, `SECURITY_HEADERS`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `DSH_UPDATE_AUTO_CHECK`, `PORTAL_SYNC`, ...);
5. browser storage keys and HTTP headers (`X-On-Behalf-User`);
6. commands, paths, code blocks, and package names (`@deepseek-ai/cordis`, `cli/dshctl.mjs`, `dsh plugin --profile web add github:01men/ybkkasi`).

YuanBingKe additionally enforces **event-source discipline** on its own bus: platform namespaces (`iam.*`, `authn.*`, `mcp.*`, `audit.*`, `platform.*`, ...) accept only internal emitters, while third-party emitters are forced to the `plugin:<id>:` prefix with a matching validated source. The authoritative per-key Chinese glossary is the internal table `docs/协议键中文对照总表.md` (280 keys, R10); English documents may paraphrase meanings but the keys themselves are never rewritten, and any new externally visible protocol key must be added to that table.

## 8. How the ecosystem evolves

The internal Chinese design baseline is `docs/internal/ecosystem-design-v1.2.md`. Read it with two flags:

| Plan step | Status |
|---|---|
| 0 — real transports (MCP HTTP, DingTalk OpenAPI) + transactional metering store | implemented, selftest-verified |
| 1 — token audience checks + plugin-namespace scopes | implemented |
| 2 — multi-tenancy minimal set + usage pipeline (schema v1, reconciliation, capability drift) | implemented |
| 3 — third-party contract, L0 declarative runtime, marketplace gate | implemented |
| 4 — multi-tenancy full isolation | implemented |
| 5 — developer identity domain + transactional journal | implemented (funds-facing parts **deprecated by M0**) |
| 6 — OIDC Provider (RS256 / JWKS) | implemented, extended by the App SSO batches |
| 7 — L0 marketplace beta with first-party supply | implemented |
| 8 — double-entry ledger | implemented as code, **commercial semantics decommissioned and sealed by M0** |
| 9 — knowledge-base-as-service / connector marketplace / compliance portal | designed; roadmap |

**Deprecated by M0 — do not quote as active plans.** The document's commercialization chapters (wallet, double-entry revenue share, model resale, subscription collection, funding-channel dependencies) were **abolished by M0 (2026-09-09)**; the document itself carries a warning banner. The surviving external posture is transparent usage metering + internal cost pass-through, and the marketplace registers all metering at zero price.

Ecosystem direction is set in the internal Chinese docs (`docs/internal/ecosystem-design-v1.2.md`, repo root `README.md`, and the batch release notes); this English set tracks them at the current baseline (2026-10-15) and flags anything that is roadmap rather than shipped.

# YuanBingKe (ybkk-AIOS) — Getting Started


This guide takes you from zero to a running, verified YuanBingKe instance: prerequisites, both install forms, first-boot baseline initialization, the first login, demo mode, quality gates, CLI first steps, and self-update basics. Production hardening (systemd units, TLS reverse proxy, supply-chain signing, remote dsh access) is summarized in Section 10 and documented fully in the internal Chinese runbook `docs/deploy-enterprise.md`.

**Interface language note:** as of the 2026-10-16 release, the runtime UI — Console（控制台）, login page, CLI output, notifications, error messages — ships with a built-in language switcher: Simplified Chinese (default), English (US), and Japanese. Switch via the top-bar selector; the preference is stored in the browser (`rq_lang`); the CLI follows `--lang` or `DSHCTL_LANG`; any string not yet covered by a dictionary gracefully falls back to Chinese. UI locations below are annotated bilingually on first mention, e.g. **Organization & Accounts（组织与账号）** — the bilingual 'English（中文原文）' annotations remain useful for navigating screenshots, on-prem deployments pinned to Chinese, and protocol-adjacent labels; browser page translation also still works. Platform logs carry server-local timestamps — convert time zones when correlating events.

## 1. Prerequisites

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Node.js ≥ **22.6** | Check with `node -v`. The server runs native TypeScript — there is **no build step** — so older Node versions cannot start it. Do not try to bypass this. (`node:sqlite` reports "Experimental" under Node 24; harmless.) |
| A terminal | bash / zsh / PowerShell all work. |
| Network access (first install only) | `npm install` fetches dependencies, including `@deepseek-ai/cordis`. |
| An existing dsh host (bundle form only) | Only for install form B below. |

## 2. Choose an install form

| Form | Command | Entry point | Choose when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Independent process** (default) | `npm install && npm start` | `http://127.0.0.1:7300` (platform's own port) | you want the standalone platform: Console + REST API + tools bridge |
| **B. dsh bundle mount** | `dsh plugin --profile web add github:01men/ybkkasi` | the dsh web port becomes the **single entry**; the YuanBingKe data plane (REST / Console SPA / docs / MCP) is mounted under the **`/rq` prefix** | you already run a dsh (DeepSeek Harness) host and want the platform mounted into it, with operations tools visible to models |

Form B installs all 25 plugin entries in one command. Verify the mount with:

```bash
dsh --profile web --dump-config   # should list the ops-* plugin entries
```

Then, in a dsh session, ask "list all MCP services and their health" — the model should call the `mcp_service_list` tool rather than answer statically. Ecosystem mechanics (single cordis instance constraint, plugin anatomy, marketplace) are in [dsh-ecosystem.md](dsh-ecosystem.md).

Both forms perform the same first-boot **baseline initialization** on an empty data directory (next section). Optional flags: `npm start -- --port 7300 --data ./data` choose the port and data directory. What lands on disk: business configuration as JSON collections with atomic persistence, plus metering/usage data in SQLite at `data/txnstore.db` (WAL + transactions). Back up the whole data directory (cold backup) — that is the complete state of the platform.

## 3. First boot: baseline initialization

On an empty data directory the platform initializes the production shape: **built-in roles + root organization + platform administrator `admin`** — and nothing else. No demo data is created.

- The `admin` password is taken from the `ADMIN_PASSWORD` environment variable. **In production, always set it explicitly**:

  ```bash
  export ADMIN_PASSWORD='<strong password>'    # PowerShell: $env:ADMIN_PASSWORD='...'
  npm start
  ```

- If `ADMIN_PASSWORD` is not set, a random password is generated once, written to `data/admin-initial-password.txt`, and printed in the boot log. Read it and take over the account immediately (Section 4).
- Successful first boot prints a baseline-initialization completion line and a "go-live three steps" guidance box in the log, then serves the Console.

Health check:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7300/api/health        # expected: {"status":"ok",...}
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7300/api/platform/bootstrap
# expected while the initial password file still exists: {"initialPasswordPending":true}
```

If you ever lose the `admin` password: either wipe the data directory and restart (re-running baseline initialization), or have an administrator holding the `iam.user.write` permission point reset it in the Console under **Organization & Accounts（组织与账号）→ Account Details（账号详情）→ Reset Password（重置口令）**.

## 4. First-login walkthrough

1. Open `http://127.0.0.1:7300` and sign in at the Console login page as `admin`.
2. While `data/admin-initial-password.txt` still exists on the server, the login page shows a yellow "first deployment" banner (driven by `initialPasswordPending`). Change the password first: top-right avatar → **Change Password（修改密码）**.
3. Delete `data/admin-initial-password.txt` on the server. Verify takeover is complete:

   ```bash
   curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7300/api/platform/bootstrap
   # expected after change + delete: {"initialPasswordPending":false}
   ```

4. Explore: the Console opens on a role workbench (pending approvals + alerts + event stream + cost trend); the **Cmd+K command palette** searches resources and jumps to pages; every detail opens in a right-side drawer. API equivalent of the overview page:

   ```bash
   curl -s -X POST localhost:7300/api/auth/login -H 'content-type: application/json' \
        -d '{"username":"admin","password":"<your password>"}'          # returns a token
   curl -s localhost:7300/api/overview -H "authorization: Bearer <token>"
   ```

5. (Optional hardening) HTTP security response headers are on by default (nosniff / SAMEORIGIN / Referrer-Policy); leave them on unless you have a specific reason: `SECURITY_HEADERS=off` disables.

## 5. Demo mode (evaluation / training only)

```bash
DEMO_SEED=1 npm start
```

Demo mode injects a complete demo dataset on first boot: a demo organization tree, demo accounts, MCP services, skills, agents, applications, and 28 days of synthetic history. All demo accounts share the password **`Ybk@2026`**:

| Demo account | Role | Intended exploration |
|---|---|---|
| `admin` | platform super administrator | everything |
| `ops` | resource administrator | MCP / skill / agent / application management |
| `hr` | organization administrator | organization / accounts / third-party sync |
| `dev` | developer | submitting skills, registering agents |
| `audit` | auditor (read-only) | audit logs and alerting |

**DingTalk mock login:** in demo mode a mock connector enables passwordless login — on the login page choose **DingTalk Scan（钉钉扫码）** and enter the mock employee ID `DD0002`. Production baselines configure no connectors, so the third-party login entry is hidden automatically.

> **Warning — never enable `DEMO_SEED=1` in production.** Demo credentials are public knowledge (they are printed in this documentation precisely because they are demo-only). The production acceptance checklist verifies that the data directory contains no demo accounts and that `Ybk@2026` cannot log in.

## 6. Quality gates

Run both gates after installation and after every upgrade. They operate on an isolated instance (separate port + separate data directory) and never touch your production data.

```bash
npm run selftest         # end-to-end functional self-test; must be all green.
                         # Assertion count is "as of the latest run" (recent runs: ≥ 1,380 assertions) —
                         # historical counts are void by design.
npm run lint:manifests   # five-face YAML validation of plugin manifests; expected: 0 red
```

The self-test covers login / RBAC and privilege escalation, freeze → token revocation chains, MCP canary / rollback / gateway authorization (including read-only constraint interception), skill malicious-submission rejection and two-tier approval, agent lifecycle and L4 single-approver execution, on-behalf-of chains, metering idempotency and reconciliation, OIDC SSO full flows, NAS and the `/mcp` endpoint, remote dsh access, and security attack drills (state / code / refresh-token replay, uniqueness-constraint conflicts).

## 7. CLI first steps

The `dshctl` CLI talks to the REST API and supports `--output json|table`, `--dry-run`, and `--yes`. Credentials come from environment variables (`DSHCTL_TOKEN` as an alternative):

```bash
export DSHCTL_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7300     # default; adjust for remote hosts
export DSHCTL_USER=admin
export DSHCTL_PASS='<your password>'

node cli/dshctl.mjs help                    # command tree (Chinese by default; --lang or DSHCTL_LANG to switch)
node cli/dshctl.mjs mcp list --output json  # first useful read
node cli/dshctl.mjs update status           # self-update state
```

The CLI covers the full surface: `mcp` / `skill` / `agent` / `app` / `nas` / `credential` / `approval` / `plugin` / `usage` / `connect` / `update` command groups. A few representative operations:

```bash
node cli/dshctl.mjs agent offline <id> --reason="consecutive failures"   # raises an L4 approval ticket
node cli/dshctl.mjs approval decide <id> --decision=approve --opinion="confirmed"
node cli/dshctl.mjs credential list                                      # machine credential inventory
```

Tip: prefer an `ops`-type account for day-to-day CLI work rather than `admin`. All high-risk operations (offline / revoke / delete) go through L4 approval tickets and are audit-trailed; preview changes with `--dry-run` first.

## 8. Platform self-update basics

Both install forms can sense new upstream releases; **the administrator always decides whether to upgrade**.

- **Automatic check** (default): every 24 h, first check 15 s after start. It compares the remote `package.json` version plus the GitHub commit delta. On a new release the Console top bar shows an **Update available（可更新）** badge and a `platform.update.available` event is emitted (audit-trailed). The Console drawer can switch checking off or change its frequency.
- **Manual upgrade:**
  - source checkout form — Console drawer **One-click upgrade（一键升级）** (runs `git pull --ff-only` + `npm install`, with dry-run preview, reason logging, and a restart prompt), or the CLI:
    `node cli/dshctl.mjs update status | check | apply [--dry-run]`;
  - bundle form — run `dsh plugin update` on the dsh host, then restart the dsh host;
  - Agent tools `update_status` / `update_check` / `update_apply` let an MCP-connected agent do the same in-session.
- **Permission points:** `platform.update.read` (view / check), `platform.update.apply` (upgrade).
- Optional supply-chain hardening — generate an Ed25519 release key pair, register the public key, and enable `requireSignedManifests` so update manifests must verify before apply — is documented in the internal runbook `docs/deploy-enterprise.md`.

## 9. Environment variable reference (quick start scope)

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ADMIN_PASSWORD` | initial `admin` password; if unset, a random one is written to `data/admin-initial-password.txt` |
| `DEMO_SEED` | `1` injects demo data on first boot — **evaluation only, never production** |
| `USAGE_RETENTION_DAYS` | usage event retention, default 730; `0` = keep permanently |
| `SECURITY_HEADERS` | `off` disables default-on HTTP security response headers |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | raises GitHub API limits for update checks |
| `DSH_UPDATE_API_BASE` / `DSH_UPDATE_RAW_BASE` | point update checks at a private mirror |
| `DSH_UPDATE_AUTO_CHECK` | `off` disables the automatic update check |
| `DSHCTL_URL` / `DSHCTL_USER` / `DSHCTL_PASS` / `DSHCTL_TOKEN` | CLI connection and credentials |

## 10. Production readiness checklist (summary)

Adapted from the internal deployment runbook; each item has a verification command there.

- [ ] `node -v` ≥ 22.6; service runs under a process supervisor (systemd unit provided in the runbook)
- [ ] `GET /` returns 200; Console login works with the `ADMIN_PASSWORD` you set
- [ ] `data/admin-initial-password.txt` deleted; `GET /api/platform/bootstrap` shows `initialPasswordPending:false`
- [ ] `npm run selftest` all green and `npm run lint:manifests` 0 red (isolated instance)
- [ ] Production data directory contains **no demo accounts**; `Ybk@2026` cannot log in
- [ ] Data directory cold-backup schedule in place
- [ ] (If dsh-mounted) `dsh --profile web --dump-config` lists the ops-* entries; agent answers `mcp list`-type questions via tools
- [ ] (Optional) update-check settings: private mirror / `GITHUB_TOKEN` / `DSH_UPDATE_AUTO_CHECK=off`; signed release manifests enabled

## 11. Troubleshooting quick table

| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
|---|---|
| Server exits at start, TypeScript cannot run | Node < 22.6 — upgrade Node; do not bypass |
| Port already in use | an orphan process holds the port — stop it before restarting (the runbook ships a port-guard script) |
| Anonymous `curl` to an unknown `/api/*` path returns 401, not 404 | by design: the auth middleware runs before routing; there is no route-existence side channel |
| DingTalk login entry missing on the login page | production baseline configures no connectors — third-party entry auto-hides; configure the DingTalk connector for real use |
| Login page shows a yellow banner | expected until the initial password is changed and `data/admin-initial-password.txt` is deleted (Section 4) |
| Agent answers from memory instead of calling tools (bundle form) | the bundle is not mounted, or a second cordis instance is loaded — re-check that `dsh --profile web --dump-config` lists the ops-* entries; see [dsh-ecosystem.md](dsh-ecosystem.md) §3.2 |
| `admin` password lost | wipe the data directory and restart, or reset via an `iam.user.write` administrator (Section 3) |
| Demo accounts missing | baseline initialization is demo-free by design; use `DEMO_SEED=1` on a fresh data directory for evaluation |
